summary: Establishes the context and goals for a Common Name Resolution Protocol, one to find resources by common names. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: People like to look things up by everyday names. This describes what a system for that would need to do.

subtitle: Context and goals for resolving everyday names to internet resources.

tldr.problem: People remember everyday names (company names, book titles, people names) better than URLs. A protocol for resolving these common names to internet resources would be useful, but its scope and requirements need to be clearly defined.
tldr.mechanism: The document establishes terminology, defines what common name resolution is, identifies use cases and business models, and sets criteria for evaluating a successful protocol.
tldr.outcome: This informational document provided the foundation for developing the Common Name Resolution Protocol (CNRP) as a lightweight alternative to full-text search for lookups by human-readable names.

facts.label: Target clients
facts.value: Browser enhancements and web search portals

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Protocol design only, excludes discovery and security

today: RFC 2972 is an Informational document establishing context and goals for CNRP development. It has not been obsoleted. CNRP (RFC 3112, published later) became the working group's protocol specification.

sections.title: Why Common Names Matter
sections.content:
People naturally remember and use common names—trade names, company names, book titles, people's names—rather than technical identifiers like URLs. A name like "Coca-Cola" is easier to remember than a URL, and most people find it frustrating to type in long web addresses.

Unlike URLs, common names lack formal syntax. A company name is just whatever people call it. Unlike URNs, common names do not need to be globally unique or permanently tied to one resource. The same name might refer to different things in different contexts. Common names are expected to be used by humans, not machines.

Common name resolution is the process of mapping a common name to internet resources. A good analogy is a dictionary. Different publishers create different dictionaries for the same language, and different resolution services can exist for the same category of names. Just as dictionaries serve different audiences, resolution services will specialize in different categories.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a dictionary but for finding things on the internet. You type in an everyday name and get back internet resources. Different companies could run different versions, like how Merriam-Webster and Oxford both publish dictionaries.

sections.title: Key Goals for the Protocol
sections.content:
The CNRP protocol should be a lightweight search protocol focused on simple, common cases. The primary goal is parameterized resolution—the ability to specify multiple attributes in a query and get results with matching attributes back. For example, searching for a company by name and country, or a book by title and author.

The protocol should support substring matches against parameter values and use UTF-8 encoding for full internationalization. To keep the protocol simple and implementable, it should avoid complex Boolean queries, relevance ranking, and other features of general-purpose search engines. The focus is on finding one or a small set of matching results, not ranking millions.

The protocol should define how clients discover what parameters a service accepts and what properties it will return, and how to express error conditions. One sample service—common name resolution itself—should be defined as a proof of concept.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol needs to be simple: you ask for a name plus a few details (like which country), and you get back matching results. No fancy search tricks, just straightforward lookup.

sections.title: Common Name Namespaces
sections.content:
A common name namespace is a set of names within a category—such as company names, book titles, people names, song titles, or place names. A private namespace is controlled by a single authority that decides which names are assigned. A public namespace is unbounded; anyone can assign names, so duplicates and ambiguity are inevitable.

Examples of use include business directories (company names to SEC filings), whitepages (people names to contact information), e-commerce directories (product descriptions), publishing (ISBN or book titles), and yellow pages (business names or addresses). The diversity of namespaces illustrates that CNRP is broadly applicable.

Public namespaces present scalability challenges. The document proposes that CNRP support categories or keywords as a filtering mechanism. For instance, a query for "antique books" could let each service map that phrase to its own category structure (whether hierarchical or flat) without requiring a global standard taxonomy. This approach preserves service independence while improving the relevance of result sets.
sections.plainLanguage: Different types of information have different name systems. Some are controlled (like company names registered with the government), others are free-form (like book titles). CNRP has to work with both.

sections.title: Deployment and Business Models
sections.content:
Two categories of organizations are expected to deploy CNRP services: web portals (search engines, Yahoo, MSN) and browser companies (Netscape, Microsoft Internet Explorer). Portals use CNRP to integrate multiple specialized lookup services into their site without maintaining custom integrations. Browser vendors embed resolution into the address bar, allowing users to type a name instead of a URL.

For CNRP to succeed, resolution services must be economically viable. The document describes five cost recovery models: licensing the lookup service to portals, sharing revenue from banner advertising on result pages, charging subscribers for registered names, offering resolution as a free value-added service tied to a core business, and offering free names in exchange for user data or email addresses for marketing.

These diverse business models suggest CNRP will see real-world deployment and use, making standardization worthwhile.
sections.plainLanguage: Search engines could use CNRP to offer company lookup alongside web search. Browsers could use it so you can type a company name in the address bar. Companies might charge for premium names or make money from ads.

sections.title: Scope and Out-of-Scope Issues
sections.content:
The document explicitly limits scope to the protocol itself. Out of scope are service discovery (how clients find resolution services), administration of services, name registration and ownership rules, and ensuring that common names are unique or persistent. Security and authentication are also identified as outside the immediate scope, though they will be important for deployment.

The protocol is designed for query-response transactions. It is not suitable for browsing, streaming, or other non-transactional uses. This focused scope keeps the protocol simple and enables rapid standardization.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol answers the question: how do you send a query for a name and get results back? It does not answer how you register a name, discover services, or keep things secure—those are other problems to solve later.
